Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 2 Purchasing 3 Resources 3.1 Base resources 3.2 In-play resource bonuses 3.3 Resource Generators 3.4 Converter huts 4 Victory Points 4.1 In-play VP's 4.2 Round-End VP's 4.3 Game-End VP's Overview You are the chieftain of a kingdom (your placemat) with up to five villages (rows). You buy or go to the islands to get place tiles that you put in your villages. There are five rounds and you get a decreasing amount of resources each round with which to acquire place tiles. Its a many-paths-to-victory kind of game. (It has been described as Stone Age without the dice). There are three kinds of resources: 1) Feet - let you move around the board, or travel to the islands or go to the cove to catch fish. 2) Clam shells - let you buy place tiles from the board 3) Fruit - can be used in place of feet or clam shells in all-or-nothing fashion. If you substitute for feet, you must substitute the entire moving cost. If you substitute for clams, you must substitute the entire purchase price. Moving: Your chieftains start at the beach and it costs nothing to return there from the board. Each movement in from the beach costs one foot. Moving up, down, right, left or diagonal on the board costs one foot per space. Staying on a space costs one foot. To go to the islands, you use your boats and feet. The closest island costs three feet and the farthest costs six. You have to have the feet as well as the space on the boats for the feet. You get an immediate victory point bonus for going to the islands but you do not get a price token (more about that later). Also, you get the level 2 version of whatever place tile or item you are getting on the islands. For instance, to go to the six foot island, you would need either: A) two three-feet boats and six feet resources or B) you would need the four-foot boat (which comes with a prepaid foot) and the two-foot boat as well as five feet resources. That is the advantage of the pre-paid foot on the four-foot boat. Purchasing To buy some thing from the board: Select the price token (round coloured circle with number inside) on the space with the place tile or item you want. If there is more than one place tile available on that space, you will be given a choice of which one you want. The movement cost will be in feet and the purchase price will be in clam shells but you can substitute either or both with fruit if you have it. You gain the price token for the round. There must be an available price token in order to purchase something from that space. You can pay double to get the level 2 version, which for most tiles is double effect. You place it in the village (row) of your choice. You must be able to place it in order to purchase it. A) You can only have one of each type of place tile in each village. For instance, you cannot have a foot (1) hut and a foot (2) hut in the same village but you can have a coconut fruit (1) tree and a breadfruit (2) tree in the same village. B) You can have only one god in each village. You can only have one of each type of god in your whole kingdom and the god vp effects are kingdom-wide. B) Each village must begin with a hut. The huts have a picture of a hut on them: foot hut, clam hut, spear hut, exchange hut, and long hut. Resources Base resources Base resources are on the round indicator. They decrease with each succeeding round. Everyone gets the base resources at the beginning of the round. Any unused resources can be used in the next round. In-play resource bonuses The third, fourth and fifth villages give you 1, 2 and 3 clams respectively when you purchase Kahunas (Hawaiian priests) for them. When you purchase for your kingdom the second, third and fourth Tikis, you are granted 1, 2, and 3 feet, respectively. One or two of the island treasures are four fruit resources. community_text:
[Rating: 2/10] Run of the mill Euro with more going on than I could possibly care about.  Ho hum.

[Rating: 2/10] Typical eurotrash. An uninteresting abstract game with a nice picture underneath.

[Rating: 2/10] Not my game. The fact that you can calculate everyone's score during the game means it's just an exercise in doing the best move at the time.  I know, many games are like that, but since you know what everyone has it's not a game to me, it's a math problem to be solved. "Player A has 15 points, Player B has 12 and I have 10. The best I can do is get 3 points for this round. That is what I do."  I agree with Tom Vasel.

[Rating: 2/10] Annoying. Have unneeded complex scoring mechanism, causing "Analysis Paralysis" in the last two rounds.

[Rating: 2/10] I thought this was pretty good. The second game we played my Wife just used my strategy from the first game and won easily. I thought that was weird because we knew exactly what she was doing and nothing we did was able to prevent it from happening. Also, I felt that going last right from the beginning seemed to put me at such a disadvantage for the rest of the game. I'm sure further plays could be better but we have so many great Euro games that there is no point.

[Rating: 2/10] If all games were like this I wouldn’t play games anymore. This isn’t just a bad game, it’s a bad way to spend time.

[Rating: 2.5/10] Was so excited when I got this game - from the reviews, the buzz, the rules, this game was destined to become a favourite game.  Sadly, a mish-mash of tried and well worn mechanics do not a good game make!  I normally do not rate games until more than 3 plays, but I am never playing this again with any number of players. I really do not see why it is so popular (and fully accept that it could just be me being dense!)

[Rating: 3/10] Nice components, but too many ways to get points (i.e., no flow), and I'm tired of these each-player-has-a-player-mat-and-you-build-your-own-village games.

[Rating: 3/10] Complex individual player boards, hidden resources, and high proportion, end-game scoring:  I hated this game at first sight.  It didn't get a fair chance from me, but probably won't.

[Rating: 3/10] The epitome of boring. This is everything that is wrong with the turn Eurogames are taking these days. I swear some guy who works at the Euro Game Mechanics factory was sweeping some leftovers off the floor and decided to package them up and sell them to us poor saps. This snoozefest could have been designed and published in 1977 and no one would have noticed.  Many of these "buzzworthy" eurogames these days make me feel like a monkey turning a gear to make colored cubes and victory points pop out of my contraption. In this one, the monkey suffers from narcolepsy.

[Rating: 3/10] Achieves the distinction of taking a beautiful place like Hawaii and that inspiration results in a dry, boring game with no color and no soul.  It seems since Agricola came out that it led to numerous cube pushing games that are overly complicated and have many non-intuitive ways to score.  What happened to games with elegantly simple rules and gameplay featuring difficult decisions?  I'll say Aloha to this one in the goodbye sense.
